findings.title: Active mixed content on an HTTPS page
findings.description: 15 resource(s) are requested over plain HTTP from a page served over HTTPS.
findings.inference: These are "active" mixed content — script and stylesheet resources fetched over an unencrypted channel. An attacker on the network path can replace them with arbitrary code that then runs with full privileges on the HTTPS page, which defeats the encryption entirely. Modern browsers block active mixed content outright, so the resources are also simply not loading.

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy header
findings.description: The `content-security-policy` response header is not set.
findings.inference: CSP is the primary defence against cross-site scripting. It tells the browser which sources are allowed to execute script, so that even if an attacker manages to inject a `<script>` tag, the browser refuses to run it. Without a policy, any successful injection executes with full privileges.
findings.technicalDetails:
Response headers observed on the document request:
  content-encoding
  content-type
  date
  etag
  last-modified
  strict-transport-security
findings.impact: This is a missing defence-in-depth control rather than an exploitable vulnerability on its own. It increases the damage another flaw could do.
findings.recommendation: Deploy a Content-Security-Policy. Start in report-only mode (`Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`) with a collection endpoint so you can see what would break before enforcing, then tighten toward `default-src 'self'` with explicit allowances.

findings.title: Server response time (TTFB) is 929 ms
findings.description: The browser waited 929 ms for the first byte of the HTML document.
findings.inference: TTFB is the time from navigation start until the first byte of HTML arrives. It is composed of DNS, connection setup, TLS, request travel, server processing, and response travel — none of which frontend code can influence. Because every other metric on the page starts counting from here, TTFB sets a floor that no amount of asset optimisation can go below.
findings.technicalDetails:
TTFB: 929 ms
Document Cache-Control: not set
findings.impact: Every visitor waits this long before anything at all can render. It is the single largest fixed cost in the page load and it affects first-time and returning visitors alike.
findings.recommendation: Add full-page or fragment caching at the origin so repeat requests are not recomputed, and put a CDN in front so the response is served from a point of presence near the user. Set an explicit `Cache-Control` header on the document so intermediaries know what they may cache.

findings.title: Weak strict-transport-security configuration
findings.description: The `strict-transport-security` header is set, but max-age is 0 seconds, below the 6-month minimum that preload lists require.

measuredFacts.label: Issue
measuredFacts.value: max-age is 0 seconds, below the 6-month minimum that preload lists require

findings.inference: HSTS instructs the browser to use HTTPS for this host for a stated period, without waiting for a redirect. It closes the window in which a first plain-http request can be intercepted and downgraded — the classic coffee-shop attack. The header is present here, but max-age is 0 seconds, below the 6-month minimum that preload lists require — so the protection it is supposed to provide is substantially reduced.
findings.technicalDetails: strict-transport-security: max-age=0; includeSubDomains; preload
findings.impact: The control is present but not providing its intended protection.
findings.recommendation: Add `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`. Roll out with a short max-age first and confirm every subdomain serves HTTPS correctly before extending it, because the directive is not easily reversible in browsers that have cached it.
